title: How to Grow Comprehension
author: Whitney Whealdon
summary: Whitney Whealdon continues her lawn metaphor for reading instruction by asking how the science of reading comprehension can be turned into classroom practice that actually grows understanding. She reviews the Simple View of Reading, Scarborough's Reading Rope and the Active View of Reading, then turns to Walter Kintsch's account of comprehension as a layered process in which readers build a mental model by linking a text to what they already know. Because the reader, the text and the purpose change each time, comprehension cannot be precisely measured, predicted or guaranteed, just as no gauge guarantees that grass will grow. She argues that instruction built around mastering discrete standards produces a weedy lawn of superficial comprehension, and that lesson design should start by studying the text and asking what makes it hard, what knowledge it demands and which relationships among ideas are difficult to see. She describes how the Louisiana ELA Guidebooks put this into practice, choosing instructional approaches to fit each text, and says assessment should build a comprehension profile across many texts rather than serve as a verdict from one score.
points: Comprehension is an active process of connecting a text to existing knowledge, so the understanding a reader stores is unique and cannot be guaranteed by any single lesson or test.
Teaching standards as a checklist of separable skills is like fixing only the watering schedule of a lawn, and it yields superficial comprehension.
Lesson design should begin with the text, asking what makes it challenging, what knowledge it requires and which relationships among ideas are hard to spot.
Rather than committing to direct instruction or discovery, designers should choose the approach, such as read aloud, paired reading or think aloud, that fits the conditions of each text.
A single assessment score reflects one reader, one text and one purpose, so teachers should read results as one piece of a longer comprehension profile.
quotes: Our continued desire for measurement precision, predictive ability, and guarantees with reading comprehension is so off, it’s not even wrong. While we can identify and measure some of the elements that contribute to comprehension, we cannot precisely predict or guarantee the understanding that results from their interaction.

Like with grass growing, there is science to back up these elements. The question, then, is: How do we translate what we know about the science of reading comprehension into instructional and assessment practices that actually support its growth?

But instead of recognizing that comprehension depends on the interaction of multiple elements, features, and conditions, we've designed our instruction and assessment around mastering individual standards.
That’s like trying to grow grass by only focusing on your watering schedule and ignoring everything else. The result for reading is superficial comprehension. That’s our weedy lawn.
This means that designing units and lessons must start with studying the texts, not identifying the standards students need to master.

Rather than committing to a particular instructional approach like direct instruction or discovery-based learning, we focused on which approach or combination of approaches would best equip students with the knowledge and habits of thinking to comprehend each text.
Their scores represented how each student handled that specific text for that specific purpose at that specific moment.

Our systems have slowly led us away from the learning we care about toward what we can most easily measure. Since comprehension is complex and hard to measure, we’ve substituted mastery of discrete skills as evidence of understanding, even as students still struggle to read and understand complex, grade-level texts.
